problems.description: 58 naming-convention violations across index.ts and cache.ts: functions not camelCase, constants not UPPER_CASE, classes/interfaces not PascalCase; drives convention score to 0.46
Cognitive complexity +50 spread across only 6 functions in a first-session greenfield commit indicates deeply nested or overloaded function bodies
10 files created with 0 classes and only 6 functions in session 1 suggests logic concentrated in a few large functions rather than decomposed modules
package-lock.json (3642 lines) committed in full; expected for a greenfield npm project but adds review noise to the session commit

strengths: Zero new bugs and no duplications introduced (duplications +0.0%)
Smells decreased by 4, so structure is an improvement over the empty baseline
Jest/ts-jest test harness configured correctly with proper moduleFileExtensions and roots
Lockfile committed with dependency set consistent with package.json bin/deps
commit_reviews.summary: A functionally clean greenfield baseline (0 bugs, -4 smells, 0% duplication) undermined by systemic naming-convention violations (score 0.46) and top-heavy functions carrying +50 cognitive complexity.

problems.description: @types/handlebars is a deprecated stub package (handlebars ships its own type definitions, per the registry deprecation notice) and is added to 'dependencies' instead of 'devDependencies'; it also drags a transitive 'handlebars: *' entry into the lockfile.

Convention score 0.46 with 58 violations: functions/classes/interfaces/constants naming rules violated across new/modified code (e.g. cache.ts: 'Functions should use camelCase', 'Classes should use PascalCase', 'Interfaces should use PascalCase', 'Constants should be UPPER_CASE'; index.ts class/interface/function naming).
Promoting handlebars to a runtime dependency expands the production dependency surface; a lighter hand-rolled renderer would have matched the existing zero-runtime-dep pattern.
The refactor swaps the existing inline HTML-builder functions for a new TemplateEngine abstraction — a pattern change imposed rather than following the established builder-function pattern.

strengths: Extracting buildPageHTML/buildIndexHTML into a TemplateEngine reduces cognitive complexity by 10 with no new bugs (SonarQube bugs +0).
The new --templates CLI flag follows the existing yargs .option(...) pattern used for --content and --output.
Introduces a clear PageTemplateData shape and per-page template/layout frontmatter support, improving extensibility for the static-site story.
commit_reviews.summary: Solid feature addition (templating via handlebars + TemplateEngine, complexity -10, no bugs) that is dragged down by a deprecated stub types package placed in runtime dependencies and widespread naming-convention violations (score 0.46, 58 violations), so it lands worse than the baseline it replaced.

problems.description: src/serve.ts serves files via path.join(outputDir, req.url) without normalization; a URL like /../ could escape the output directory (dev-server only, so limited blast radius)
Request handler uses blocking fs.existsSync/statSync/readFileSync on every request instead of async fs.promises; acceptable for a dev server but serializes the event loop
+478 lines of new server logic (HTTP, WebSocket, file watching) shipped without any tests for serve.ts

Convention score 0.46 with 58 naming violations; DISCREPANCY: many flagged lines (cache.ts, index.ts) are not in this diff, and the rules applied (camelCase functions + PascalCase interfaces simultaneously) contradict TS idioms — the analyzer appears to be applying mixed/Python-centric rules, so the low score overstates the commit's own violation count

strengths: New serve module integrates cleanly through the existing build() function and yargs command pattern rather than bypassing them
Dependencies (chokidar, ws, @types/ws) declared in both package.json and package-lock.json consistently
SonarQube deltas all positive: smells -14, cognitive complexity -11, duplications -7.7%, bugs 0
serve() takes an explicit ServeOptions object matching the existing config-object pattern and exposes a testable ServeInstance interface
commit_reviews.summary: Solid architectural integration that reuses the existing build() and CLI command pattern, but the mechanical convention score of 0.46 is largely pre-existing or analyzer-misapplied, with the commit's own additions mostly idiomatic TS aside from minor path-traversal, sync-IO, and missing-test gaps.

problems.description: BuildContext and SSGConfig leak `any` (`[key: string]: any`, `Record<string, any>`), undermining type safety across the plugin boundary — this is the seam every plugin passes through.

DevServerPlugin bypasses the lifecycle it itself defines: it exposes `start()`/`setEngine()`/`getInstance()` instead of implementing behavior in onStart/afterBuild, so the dev server is not driven through the plugin contract.
rebuild() swallows all build errors with a `// nop` catch, so failures during live-reload rebuilds are silently masked and hard to diagnose.
DevServerPlugin imports the concrete SSGEngine class from '../ssg' rather than an interface, coupling the plugin layer to the engine implementation and creating an implicit setEngine wiring step.
Mechanical convention score is 0.46 with 58 violations; listed ones in index.ts (PascalCase/camelCase/UPPER_CASE) and cache.ts are touched by this refactor and were not cleaned up.
No test files are added or updated for the new plugin modules despite the refactor moving core build behavior (markdown parsing, templating, serving) behind plugins.

strengths: Clean separation of concerns: markdown, template, and dev-server concerns are extracted behind a lifecycle-hook plugin interface (onStart/beforeBuild/onFile/afterBuild/onEnd).
SonarQube deltas are all positive: -4 smells, -46 cognitive complexity, -2.1% duplications, +0 bugs.
Plugin modules are small, focused, and readable with clear single responsibilities.
commit_reviews.summary: Refactor net-improves the codebase (complexity -46, smells -4, dups -2.1%, no new bugs) by extracting a plugin system, but weak `any` typing, a dev-server plugin that bypasses its own lifecycle, silent error swallowing, and a low convention score (0.46, driven by violations in the index.ts/cache.ts files this commit touches) leave real maintainability debt.

compounding_issues: No .gitignore ever created: dist/ and node_modules/ committed in every session, making session 1 alone ~968K insertions across 5153 files and bloating all subsequent diffs
Session 1's hardcoded inline HTML (buildPageHTML/buildIndexHTML) was a throwaway design that session 2 replaced wholesale with the Handlebars engine — dead-end code, wasted effort
Plugin config loading (sessions 4-5) probes process.cwd()/__dirname with a runtime require() of a .ts config — fragile, best-effort surface with no test coverage
key_decisions: Session 1 fixed the foundation: marked + gray-matter + yargs + strict TypeScript + jest, and a build-only CLI
Session 2 introduced a Handlebars TemplateEngine class (default layouts, per-page templates, partials) replacing hardcoded HTML
Session 3 added a chokidar + ws dev server with WebSocket live-reload injection behind npx ssg serve, without breaking build

Session 4 extracted a plugin system (Plugin interface with onStart/beforeBuild/onFile/afterBuild/onEnd hooks, built-in Markdown/Template/DevServer plugins, ssg.config.ts), collapsing serve.ts to a thin wrapper
Session 5 added a CacheManager content-hash manifest with --incremental/--clean flags and build stats, preserving the plugin pipeline
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily and monotonically. Session 1 produced a functional but monolithic SSG with hardcoded string HTML; session 2 was the largest quality jump, swapping that dead-end markup for a proper Handlebars engine with layouts and partials while refactoring ssg.ts; session 3 integrated a live-reload dev server cleanly; session 4 was a behavior-preserving architectural refactor that matured the codebase into a hook-based plugin pipeline without breaking any existing tests; session 5 layered incremental caching on top, keeping the plugin architecture intact. Test coverage grew from 137 to ~961 lines across the arc, and every session honored the 'don't break existing functionality' constraint, so the code moved from a monolith to a modular, extensible, cache-aware generator.
story_review.summary: A highly coherent, quality-ascending 5-session arc — greenfield monolith → template engine → dev server → plugin architecture → caching — marred only by repo-hygiene debt (committed node_modules/dist) and a throwaway session-1 HTML layer.
